display.title: The Wondrous Glasses of Lemberg and a Blood Libel in France
display.summary_short: Two Yiddish stories: how a blind boy in Lemberg found glasses that let him see and gave the Brill family its name, and the start of a blood libel in France.
display.summary_long: Told in Yiddish. About two hundred years ago in Lemberg, a respected family is blessed with a baby boy, Michoel, but the doctors find he was born blind. He grows up learning everything by heart, knows the whole siddur and Mishnayos, and loves to hold and kiss sefarim. One day in the big beis midrash he takes down a dusty old sefer and finds a small case of glasses between its pages. When he puts them on, he can see. He keeps the secret for a few days, then tells his family, learns to read, and becomes a great talmid chacham. People call him 'Michoel Brillen' because he keeps asking whose glasses they were, and the name stays with the family. He marries, succeeds in business and gives much tzedakah. After he passes away, his children argue over the glasses, which fall and shatter. The narrator teaches that we thank Hashem each morning for our sight and should use it for Torah, davening and helping others. A second story begins: in France two gentiles accuse the Jews of murder, Jewish leaders are jailed, and a visiting ambassador from Turkey tells the king how absurd the blood libel is. The recording ends before the outcome.
display.lesson: Our eyesight is a gift from Hashem: thank Him for it every morning and use it to learn Torah, daven and help other Jews.

advisories.note: A blood libel in France: Jewish leaders are jailed and tortured to force a confession.
The hero of the first story passes away in old age.
